title: Thinking deeply about retrieval: context
author: Jo Castelino
summary: Castelino argues that Do Now retrieval questions should be chosen for their relevance to the lesson about to be taught rather than simply drawn from any prior content. Using a photosynthesis sequence, she compares two sets of starter questions and explains why the second set activates the knowledge, such as chloroplasts, starch and energy flow, that the new learning will build on. She admits she made the opposite mistake for years, and warns that retrieval for its own sake can overload working memory and distract from the current sequence. Unrelated retrieval is moved to independent practice and homework, with reteaching when forgetting shows up. She grounds the approach in schema theory and the idea that pupils learn their interpretation of what is taught. The bucket is Learning & Curriculum because it applies cognitive science to lesson design.
points: Retrieval questions should activate the specific prior knowledge the new lesson depends on, not just any earlier content.
Retrieval for retrieval's sake can overload working memory and divert attention from the current learning sequence.
Unrelated retrieval questions belong in independent practice and homework, with reteaching when gaps appear.
Setting context in the Do Now helps pupils build schemas and interpret connections, since they otherwise may miss the intended meaning.
quotes: Retrieval for retrieval’s sake can cause more problems than it solves. It can cause students’ working memories to be overloaded and make it harder for them to consider the current learning sequence.

If the answer does not link in with the current learning, and then students don’t get it right, we run the risk of focusing our students’ thinking on something that is still important but not immediately relevant.
Once again, it is better to choose a questions that sets the focus of the lesson and allows the new learning to be put in context of previous learning.

I used to think it was fine to add in a question that wasn’t linked to the current learning at all but after finding my low prior attaining groups struggle to focus on one thing instead of 2 or 3 different topics covered all at once, I’ve changed my mind.

Now I incorporate those questions in independent practice after students have practised their current learning and I also set them for homework. When reviewing homework, if I find that students have clearly forgotten something, I make time in a future lesson to cover that bit and reteach it.

Having the context in place for Do Now retrieval questions means that I am helping my students build their schemas and I am guiding them in accurately interpreting the connections between their knowledge.

Pupils don’t learn what you teach; they learn their interpretation of what you teach. For pupils lacking in knowledge of a topic, this means they can totally miss the meaning you want them to make from a text/example/demonstration/explanation unless you explicitly tell them what to focus on.
